text: So, in the previous part, we looked at how protests over conditions in French high schools developed into a nationwide movement accompanied by serious violence. And now I want to focus on probably the most controversial questions surrounding these events. Who are the people actually committing the violence? Are they mostly high school students, immigrants and their descendants, radical left activists, or as Donald Trump and some other commentators have suggested, Islamists? And I think the first thing worth looking at is what the official statistics actually tell us. Who are the people being arrested? According to the French Ministry of Justice, by October 14th, 7,950 people had been placed in police custody in connection with violence surrounding the high school protest movement. And here's something interesting. Approximately 85% of them were minors. So we are talking about almost 6,800 people under the age of 18. Now, that doesn't mean all of those teenagers were high school students. And it certainly doesn't mean all of them were guilty of rioting. Being placed in police custody is not the same as being convicted of a crime. In fact, the authorities didn't even specify exactly what proportion were suspected of committing violence, as opposed to other offenses connected with the protests. But the figures do tell us something important. During the earlier stages of the unrest, the people placed in police custody were overwhelmingly minors. However, something interesting happened during the much more violent demonstrations on October 17th. According to the Ministry of Justice, around 2,700 people were placed in police custody following those demonstrations and the subsequent unrest. And this time, according to a ministry spokesperson speaking on October 20th, approximately 70% were adults, while only 30% were minors. So the age profile had almost completely reversed. And in Paris, the difference was even more pronounced. According to the Paris prosecutor, depending on the reporting date and the count, adults accounted for roughly 78% to 90% of the custody cases. Now, these statistics cover different stages of the unrest, and we shouldn't assume that everyone detained actually committed violence. These tactics and the types of offenses being investigated may also affect who gets arrested. But this is still a substantial difference, and it suggests that the composition of people being detained changed as the protests expanded. Which makes sense, considering that by October 17th, the demonstrations were no longer primarily about high school conditions. They had attracted university students, trade unions, yellow vest activists, and other groups protesting against the cost of living and government policies. So we might actually be dealing with different groups of people with different motivations participating in what is often presented as one continuous wave of riots. And what do we know about these adults? Well, we have some additional information. On October 22nd, the Ministry of Justice reported that 217 people had been incarcerated following the violence of October 17th and 18th. And the Ministry analysis examined 186 people incarcerated between October 18th and 21st. According to that analysis, 95% were men, 68% were aged 25 or younger, and 52% had no previous criminal record. But there's another statistic that's particularly relevant to our question. Approximately 70% were French nationals, while around 30% were foreign nationals. Now, to put that into perspective, according to France's National Statistics Institute, foreign nationals made up approximately 9% of the country's population in 2025. So the proportion of foreign nationals in this particular incarcerated group was considerably higher than their share of the general population. And I think that's worth acknowledging. However, there are some important limitations. First, these 186 individuals were not a representative sample of everyone who participated in the riots. They were people who ended up in prison, which is a much more selective group. Second, foreign nationals are also overrepresented in certain categories of recorded crime in France, particularly theft, even outside these protests. And according to a recent fact-check by Le Surligneur, the proportion of foreign nationals among suspects in some of the October 17th offenses was broadly comparable to the proportions ordinarily recorded for similar offenses. So these figures don't by themselves demonstrate that immigration caused this particular wave of violence. And finally, nationality is not the same as ethnicity or religion. A French national can be a child or grandchild of immigrants. A foreign national can come from another European country. And neither nationality tells us whether someone is Muslim, let alone an Islamist. France also doesn't routinely publish racial or religious breakdowns of arrested individuals, although research into people's origins is possible under certain conditions. So we don't have reliable nationwide statistics showing what proportion of these rioters were Arab, Black, White, Muslim, or anything else. And without those figures, I don't think we can confidently establish the ethnic or religious composition of the rioters. Of course, we can still investigate the available evidence. Which brings us to the question of Islamist involvement. Were Islamists involved? First, I think it's important to distinguish between being Muslim and being an Islamist. A Muslim is someone who follows Islam. Islamism, on the other hand, is a political ideology seeking to shape government or society according to Islamic principles. And Islamist movements vary considerably in their goals and methods. Not all Islamists support violence, and being Muslim certainly doesn't make someone an Islamist. So when someone claims that these are Islamist riots, I think we should expect evidence that the violence was motivated or organized around Islamist political or religious goals. And there actually have been some disturbing incidents involving references to Islamist terrorists. For example, in early October, videos circulated showing teenagers at Francois Vion High School in Beaujean-Cy singing a song by a rapper called Boro Setsan. The lyrics reference Mohamed Merat, the Islamist terrorist who murdered seven people in France in 2012, including three children and a teacher at a Jewish school. They also reference Salah Abdeslam, who was convicted for his role in the November 2015 terrorist attacks in Paris. Three minors were placed in police custody in connection with the video as authorities investigated possible glorification of terrorism. There was another incident in Soulang, where teenagers were filmed singing the same song inside the church. That prompted a separate investigation. The rapper himself appeared in court on October 21st, where prosecutors requested a one-year suspended prison sentence. His defense disputed that the song was intended to glorify terrorism. Now, I don't think we should minimize this incident. Teenagers singing lyrics that appear to glorify terrorists who murder children is deeply disturbing. But what exactly do these incidents establish? They establish that some teenagers involved in or around the unrest repeated lyrics referencing jihadist terrorists. What they don't establish is that the nationwide protest movement was organized by Islamists or that most of the people committing violence were motivated by Islamist ideology. What about the Arabic slogans? There's another example that I find particularly interesting. You might have seen French protesters repeating the phrase, Bismillah, salut et nabr. Now, Bismillah is Arabic for in the name of God. But the story behind this particular phrase is rather different from what you might expect. According to Euronews, it became popular after screenshots circulated of somebody apparently trying to infiltrate Snapchat groups used by students to organize blockades. The person used a rather bizarre combination of Arabic expressions and French used slang. Some students suspected that it was an undercover police officer doing a terrible job of pretending to be one of them. Now, that suspicion has never been verified. We don't actually know who was behind the account. But the students began mocking the awkward wording and the phrase eventually became a meme. So what might initially look like a religious slogan actually appears to be a joke. And this is a good example of why context matters. The same applies to Palestinian flags, which have also appeared at some demonstrations. Supporting Palestine isn't the same as supporting Islamism. And carrying a Palestinian flag doesn't automatically tell us someone's religion or views on political violence. More importantly, I haven't found evidence that the nationwide student organizations were demanding Islamic law or religious government. Their publicly reported demands concern education, school funding, and increasingly broader social and economic issues. So what about the radical left? Now, this explanation has received considerable attention from the French government and right-wing politicians. And here we do have documented evidence of radical left involvement in the protest movement. In early October, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecarnu's office accused La France Insoumise and other left-wing organizations of helping to organize the unrest. The government referred to information from police intelligence services. And Le Mans subsequently examined a police intelligence report dated September 28th concerning school protests in Saint-Saint-Denis, a department in the Paris metropolitan area. The report described university activists distributing communist leaflets, encouraging blockades, and participating in demonstrations. But here's an interesting detail. Of the 27 protest actions examined in the report, intelligence officers recorded the presence of trade unionists, university students, or left-wing politicians on only six occasions. And the report covered just part of one department, not the entire country. And Le Mans also reported that other intelligence services offered a somewhat different explanation. According to one source, the movement initially developed spontaneously, then attracted groups of young people from disadvantaged neighborhoods, some of whom engaged in violence. Radical left organizations became more involved afterwards. And there's another detail worth mentioning. On October 20th, the Paris prosecutor said that among the cases her office had examined following the October 17th riots, none of the suspects had claimed a political motive for the acts being prosecuted. Now, that doesn't establish that none of them were politically motivated, but it does suggest that assigning political motives to every rioter isn't particularly straightforward. However, there's also a more recent development. The Limoges City Hall fire. Remember the historic city hall in Limoges that was set on fire during the October 17th riots? Well, investigators have since identified two suspects who were formally charged on October 23rd. The main suspect is a 34-year-old man whom French intelligence services have flagged for alleged links to the radical far-left, including radical environmentalist activism. According to investigators, he allegedly started the fire by throwing a burning rubbish bin through a window. The fire spread through the building and eventually caused the collapse of its 43-meter-high bell tower. He has also been charged with the attempted murder of police officers who had taken refuge inside the building. Now, these are allegations, not convictions. His lawyers dispute the evidence and intend to challenge their charges. And we don't know whether his alleged political associations had anything to do with his actions. But this is still relevant evidence when discussing the possible involvement of individuals associated with radical political movements. And what about opportunistic criminals? Well, remember the Ministry of Justice analysis of those 186 incarcerated people? It actually identified several different profiles. Approximately 46% were primarily associated with looting, 26% with confrontations against police, and another 10% with both. The remaining cases involved other offenses. Now, these categories describe alleged criminal conduct, not necessarily political motivation. But they suggest that at least some of the violence involved people interested in stealing from businesses rather than advancing any particular political or religious cause. And we should also consider that these categories can overlap. Someone can come from an immigrant family, live in a disadvantaged neighborhood, and support radical left politics. Another person with a similar background might have no particular political beliefs and simply want to steal something from a shop. So trying to explain every act of violence with one label might not get us very far. And finally, what about the viral videos? There's one more problem with relying on social media to understand these events. Some widely circulated videos supposedly showing the current riots weren't filmed during this protest at all. For example, footage showing violent clashes in Paris actually came from demonstrations following the killing of three Kurdish people in December 2022. Another video of a burning school bus was filmed in January 2023. And fact-checkers have also identified misleading AI-generated images and footage associated with both criticism of the rioters and criticism of the police. Now, this doesn't mean the current violence is fictional. There's plenty of authentic footage showing real destruction, looting, and clashes. But if someone uses a video from four years ago to support their claims about what's happening today, that should probably make us question how carefully they've checked the rest of their evidence. So where does that leave us? Based on what I've examined so far, the unrest appears to involve different groups of people and its composition seems to have changed as the protests expanded. There are reports of people from immigrant backgrounds participating in the unrest and foreign nationals made up a substantial minority of one group of incarcerated suspects. There have also been genuine incidents involving references to Islamist terrorists, as well as documented involvement by radical left activists and allegations against an individual associated with radical environmentalism. And the available criminal justice data indicate that looting and confrontations with police were both important features of the later violence. But what I haven't found is convincing evidence that the nationwide unrest was organized by Islamists or that Islamist political goals were driving most of the violence. And we still don't have reliable figures establishing what proportion of all the rioters belong to any particular ethnic, religious, or political group. So when someone describes all of this as nothing more than innocent schoolchildren protesting, I think that clearly lives out a lot. But claiming that France is experiencing an Islamist uprising also goes considerably beyond what the available evidence establishes. And I think the change in the age profile of those detained is particularly important because it suggests that we may be combining several different forms of unrest into one story. So I don't think there's one simple answer to the question of who is behind France's riots. And I understand that different people with different motivations at different stages isn't exactly a catchy political slogan. But based on what I've examined, that's much closer to what the available evidence actually allows us to say.
